title: 2026-03-04 Technical deep dive: model tuning (Llama/Mistral/Qwen) & MoE/RoPE

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~56m | Attendees: Priya Nair (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Ellen Zhou (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Product) -- Michael Chen (AeroData), Laura Kim (AeroData), Diego Ramos (AeroData), Nina Patel (AeroData)

Summary (auto): technical deep dive into model-specific tuning for Llama/Mistral/Qwen, MoE routing costs and RoPE scaling.

[00:00:05] Priya: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros - i'm priya, i'm the AE, samir and ellen are gonna lead the deep dive today.
[00:00:22] Michael: thanks, yea we wanna understand perf tradeoffs, especially if we go Dedicated or bring Redwood Private into our VPC. latency targets are sub-60ms p50 for common paths.
[00:00:35] Samir: ok great, we'll start with a quick baseline - Llama family has a fastpath we lean on for shorter sequences and small batch sizes; that reduces kv cache pressure if you can constrain seq len.
[00:00:52] Laura: when you say fastpath is that quantization safe? our stack needs int8 for cost.
[00:01:05] Samir: good q. generally int8 works but watch layernorm/softmax numerical issues - we recommend per-channel calibration and mixed-precision for critical layers. we'll share a config.
[00:01:30] Ellen: for Mistral, memory layout matters - fused kernels and tensor ordering can impact throughput a lot; we see 10-20% perf swing with different transpose strategies.
[00:01:48] Diego: any gotchas with Qwen? we have some Qwen-7B workloads.
[00:02:02] Samir: Qwen's attention matmuls are sensitive to sequence packing; batching helps throughput but may increase p99. for low-latency paths use small batches and aggressive KV caching.
[00:02:25] Priya: quick topic split - we'll cover kv cache sizing, batching heuristics, quantization tradeoffs, MoE-specific routing overhead, and RoPE scaling drift.
[00:02:43] Michael: perfect. on kv cache, our workload has many short prefixes and then longer completion; how do we size caches?
[00:02:58] Samir: typical approach is LRU per model-shard with a prefix-aware eviction; for Llama-13B we recommend keeping last N prefixes in memory - depends on your token distribution. if you have many concurrent users, consider sharding cache by user or route.
[00:03:20] Laura: do you have numbers - like how much memory per token per model?
[00:03:30] Samir: ballpark for 13B with kv cache is ~0.5-1.0 bytes per token per head per layer depending on quantization and packing; that's rough but gives dimensioning guidance.
[00:03:48] [00:04:05] Ellen: for MoE models, routing creates hotspots - the top-k router may send a disproportionate load to certain experts which inflates tail latency. you need capacity buffers and maybe a soft-routing fallback.
[00:04:24] Michael: is routing cost mostly compute or memory?
[00:04:29] Samir: both - routing adds extra scatter/gather and additional expert compute; network costs go up with cross-device expert placement. if you host on dedicated GPUs, collocate experts to reduce interconnect hops.
[00:04:48] Diego: what about token recycling / kv cache warmup when the route changes?
[00:04:54] Samir: you lose some cache locality when tokens trigger different experts; for MoE we recommend per-expert kv caches and a cache-aware routing policy to keep hot sequences on the same expert.
[00:05:12] [00:05:35] Laura: RoPE scaling - we've seen generation drift when using longer contexts, anything to watch for?
[00:05:42] Ellen: yes, RoPE scaling (positional embedding extrapolation) can cause coherence issues at longer seq lengths. There are per-model recommended RoPE scaling factors; with Llama variants you may need linear scaling adjustments or rotary decay fixes.
[00:06:03] Michael: does Redwood runtime handle RoPE adjustments automatically?
[00:06:08] Samir: we have runtime hooks that can apply RoPE scaling maps at load time, but there are tradeoffs. automatic scaling can slightly change logits distribution - we flag those in our performance/eval dashboards so you can QA.
[00:06:26] [00:06:50] Priya: moving on to batching - what's your p50/p95 targets and qps?
[00:06:55] Michael: p50 60ms target, p95 under 350ms, peak qps around 1200 across cluster.
[00:07:06] Samir: at 1200 qps you'll need batching for throughput. We recommend dynamic batching with latency budgets: e.g., 6ms or 10ms batching window for best tradeoff. For Llama-13B we measured throughput gains of 2.5x going from bs1 to bs8 in some setups.
[00:07:30] Diego: that batching window adds latency - can Redwood route low-latency traffic to dedicated low-batch nodes?
[00:07:38] Priya: yes, routing policies can split traffic by latency class - we can pin certain routes to low-batch, low-latency pools and others to cost-optimized high-batch pools.
[00:07:51] [00:08:15] Laura: on quantization, our security/compliance team wants deterministic outputs for audits - do low-bit quant models change outputs significantly?
[00:08:23] Samir: lower-bit quant (4-bit) can change outputs; int8 with per-channel calibration tends to preserve quality more. we also recommend running eval prompt sets and registering regression alerts in Redwood Optimize before deploying.
[00:08:41] Michael: any automation for choosing quant levels per layer?
[00:08:45] Ellen: we have heuristics and automated sims that suggest which layers to keep in fp16 vs quantize; some layers (like first and last) often kept in higher precision. we'll share a sample config.
[00:09:00] [00:09:25] Samir: on VPC/on-prem - network egress and inter-node latency are big for MoE and heavy batching. if you're air-gapped, you'll want Dedicated GPU pools within the VPC or Redwood Private install; we can provide a terraform template and an SRE runbook.
[00:09:46] Diego: what about KMS/HSM for keys?
[00:09:49] Priya: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; we'll include that in the security pack.
[00:09:58] [00:10:22] Michael: curious about cost math - what are the dominant cost drivers when you optimize for throughput?
[00:10:30] Samir: GPU-hours dominate, then memory for kv caches and interconnect overhead for MoE; batching reduces per-token GPU cost but increases latency. Quantization reduces memory and can cut per-token cost substantially but might push you to higher compute due to dequant/depack overhead if not done carefully.
[00:10:56] [00:11:15] Ellen: we also account for kernel selection - sometimes using a slightly older kernel yields better single-thread latency at small batch sizes; the runtime chooses kernels per-profile but you can pin them for reproducibility.
[00:11:32] [00:11:50] Laura: any recommendations for model-specific tuning checklist we can run on-prem?
[00:11:55] Samir: yes - we'll send a checklist: run seq-len sweeps, batch size sweeps, measure p50/p95/p99, evaluate kv cache hit rates, run quantization simulations, and check RoPE drift with longer contexts. also test MoE routing skew under synthetic hot-keys.
[00:12:20] [00:12:40] Michael: about benchmarks - can we get a baseline run you already have for Llama-13B and Mistral-7B?
[00:12:45] Priya: yes we'll upload our internal spreadsheets and then run an AeroData-specific sim.
[00:12:56] [00:13:10] Diego: network: if experts are cross-gpu, do you recommend NVLink colo or PCIe?
[00:13:16] Samir: NVLink helps a lot for cross-device expert traffic; without it you'll pay high latency for all-to-all. For on-prem, prefer collocated experts with NVLink or use multi-host optimizations.
[00:13:34] [00:13:54] Ellen: small note - for Qwen variants some kernels are auto-vectorized by compilers differently; we suggest testing on your hardware matrix. we'll include compiler flags we use.
[00:14:10] Michael: what's the typical improvement from quant+batching combined?
[00:14:16] Samir: combined you can see 3-6x effective per-token cost reduction relative to fp16 bs1 depending on sequence length and model family. caveat: MoE and long-context workloads often see smaller multipliers.
[00:14:35] [00:15:00] Laura: security question again - do audit logs capture per-token metadata? we need to trace prompts for compliance.
[00:15:06] Priya: Redwood Console captures request-level metadata and we can surface token counts and model versions; per-token content retention is configurable per your retention policy and privacy needs.
[00:15:20] [00:15:48] Michael: back to RoPE - do you recommend extrapolation tricks or re-embedding?
[00:15:53] Ellen: generally try RoPE extrapolation with careful eval, but re-embedding for very long contexts can be more robust at the cost of compute. We'll show both patterns.
[00:16:10] [00:16:35] Diego: for on-prem pilot, the network ops team needs a list of ports and firewall rules.
[00:16:40] Ellen: we'll attach a runbook with exact ports (gRPC endpoints, metrics, KMS endpoints).
[00:16:54] [00:17:20] Priya: any concerns from your side we haven't covered?
[00:17:25] Michael: timeline: we want to decide Dedicated vs Private in ~3 weeks - need perf numbers and security pack to make the call.
[00:17:35] Priya: understood; that's in the next steps.
[00:17:50] [00:18:10] Samir: quick technical aside on MoE cost accounting - when you do planning, account for expert over-provision factor (we usually recommend 1.2-1.5x headroom) to account for routing skew and SLOs.
[00:18:29] Michael: can Redwood runtime throttle routing? we want graceful degradation rather than hard failures.
[00:18:34] Samir: yes, soft-routing fallbacks exist: route to nearest compatible expert or fallback to dense model variant. that's part of graceful degradation.
[00:18:50] [00:19:15] Laura: for the eval harness, do you support prompt-level regression detection?
[00:19:21] Priya: Redwood Optimize ties to eval sets and can flag quality regressions as we roll quantized or new kernels.
[00:19:40] [00:19:58] Michael: ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[00:20:05] Priya: recap: Samir runs benchmarks; Ellen prepares on-prem runbook; Priya shares security and quant docs; Michael provides workload traces; follow-up pilot kickoff next week.
[00:20:25] Diego: thanks, that's good.
[00:20:40] Priya: any final q's? otherwise we'll close.
[00:20:45] Nina: minor point about SDK timeouts - we saw some 504s when batching window is too long.
[00:20:52] Samir: noted - tuning client timeouts against batching windows is part of the recommended checklist.
[00:21:05] [00:21:30] Priya: ok thanks everyone, we'll upload artifacts and send calendar invite for pilot kickoff.
[00:21:40] Michael: thanks all.

(Transcript end - remaining minutes used for side conversations and follow-up scheduling; recording stopped at 16:26 UTC)
